questions.prompt: How do you read the current value of a signal named total?
questions.explanation: A signal is a getter function — call it with parentheses to read its value, both in templates and TypeScript.

questions.prompt: Which methods change the value of a writable signal? (Select all that apply.)
questions.explanation: .set() replaces the value and .update() derives the next value from the current one. There is no .mutate() method.

options.text: A writable signal you change with .set()
A read-only signal derived from other signals; lazy and memoized
A way to run side effects like logging

questions.explanation: computed() creates a read-only signal that recalculates automatically, only when a dependency changes, and caches its result.

options.text: Deriving new state from existing signals
Side effects that reach outside Angular state, like logging or persistence

questions.explanation: Reserve effect() for true side effects; use computed() to keep derived state in sync.

questions.prompt: Which method converts a writable signal into a read-only view for safe exposure from a service?
questions.explanation: Keep the writable signal private and expose this._state.asReadonly() so consumers can read but not overwrite it.

questions.prompt: Why does items().push(item) often fail to update the UI?

options.text: push() is not a valid array method
Signals compare with Object.is, so mutating in place keeps the same reference and detects no change
Arrays cannot be stored in signals

questions.explanation: Because comparison uses Object.is, you must produce a new array, e.g. items.update(curr => [...curr, item]).

items.text: Read the current value with count()
